intro.text: One team issue inbox was written in fourteen UI frameworks, and the bias is the point. Each section speaks as that framework's biggest fan, showing why people reach for it. Every framework has value. The limits sit beside the praise so a reader can pick what fits them, and the charts show the numbers.

app.name: team inbox
app.about: One app, written once in each framework from the same spec: 10 000 issues in a virtualised list, search, a validated edit form, a weekly chart, light and dark, English and Japanese. Every implementation was driven by the same scripted session on the same machine. Each app was written by an AI coding agent, one per framework; the Ljós one by the comparison's lead, who also wrote the harness that measured them all.

frameworks.name: Ljós
frameworks.language: Ljós's QML dialect and TypeScript, on Rust

prose.fan: You reach for Ljós when you want apps that people and their agents can inspect, drive, and reshape while they run. Interfaces are declarative with reactive bindings, scripts are typed TypeScript checked before anything runs, and existing QML runs as a way in.
cool: The inbox needs no third-party dependencies because models, controls, PO translations with plurals, and AccessKit accessibility are built into the toolkit.

The store declares its state with types taken from the TypeScript module, and because a binding is re-evaluated when what it reads changes, sorting runs only when the records or the sort change and a key typed into the search only filters.
Every running app can be inspected and driven over MCP, ljos observe shows the same in a window, and dev mode reloads code on save.
limits: It is pre-1.0 at version 0.0.0 with no published release, a repo started on 2026-10-10, and no third-party libraries to speak of.

Writing the inbox turned up six findings about Ljós that needed workarounds in app code, including translated arrays stuck in their first language, a TabBar binding loop, a missed type check, and Promises unable to carry cooperative loading.
A keyed ListView copies every field of each row's record, forcing slim key objects, and the inbox rows animate opacity and position without the requested height change.
RTL layout, iOS support, production bundles, and a wgpu renderer remain unfinished milestone M4 work, and AT-SPI output was not verified for the inbox.

shows.caption: State: typed properties and a chain of derived bindings
shows.code:
property list<Inbox.Issue> all: []
property Inbox.Sort sort: "updated"
property Inbox.Filter filter: "inbox"
property string query: ""
property int selectedId: -1
// 0 Conversation, 1 Edit, 2 Insights.
property int tab: 0
// "light", "dark" or "system".
property string look: "system"
// Starts as the system's setting; the settings dialog changes it.
property bool reduced: Motion.reduced

    || (store.look === "system" && App.hints.colorScheme === ColorScheme.Dark)
// The order is worked out when the records or the sort change; a key
// typed in the search only filters it.
readonly property list<Inbox.Issue> ordered: Inbox.sorted(store.all, store.sort)
readonly property Inbox.Shown shown: Inbox.shown(store.ordered, store.filter, store.query)
readonly property list<Inbox.Issue> matches: store.shown.issues
readonly property list<Inbox.Key> rows: store.shown.keys
readonly property int selectedIndex: Inbox.indexOf(store.rows, store.selectedId)
readonly property Inbox.Issue selected: store.selectedId <= 0 ? Inbox.none : Inbox.pick(store.all, store.selectedId)

frameworks.name: Ljós on the web
frameworks.language: Ljós's QML dialect and TypeScript, compiled to Solid

prose.fan: You reach for ljos-web when you want the same declarative Ljós and TypeScript app to run in the browser without rewriting it. At build time, qmlc compiles each file to a Solid component with nothing interpreting QML at run time, and WebAssembly is used only for the opt-in kernel and 3D.
cool: The native inbox compiled with no errors or warnings on the first build and kept its pinned layout, chart, dialog, themes, and both languages.
Keeping the DOM preserves the web's accessibility tree, text input, selection, find-in-page, and scrolling, with only 17 rows in the tree at 7 017 records.
Built-in translations compile into ICU MessageFormat backed by PO catalogues, with ja.po built as a lazily loaded chunk and languages switched at run time.
Hot reload keeps typed text, assigned state, and focus across saves, and the web inspector answers in the same shapes as the native one.
limits: It is pre-1.0 at version 0.0.0 with no tagged release, the pages read give no browser support matrix, and no third-party component libraries are named.
ListView enter, exit, and displaced transitions compile without warning yet do nothing on the web, so inserted and removed rows appear and vanish at once.
File paths built at run time are missed silently by the site builder, requiring 24 literal url properties for avatars and a script to write the site manifest.
The selected-row marker and sort popup options were not verified in the accessibility snapshot, and RTL support is unstated.

shows.caption: Tab panel motion: Behaviors on opacity and position

prose.fan: You reach for Qt Quick when you want a GPU-accelerated toolkit developed since 1995 across desktop, mobile, embedded, and web. C++ handles models and logic while QML gives you declarative bindings, transitions, controls, localization, and accessibility.
cool: The inbox needed no third-party libraries, pairing C++ list and sort-filter models, locale collation, and a virtualised ListView with declarative QML views.
Live translation is built in: the C++ app installs the translator, sets the default locale, gives the sort proxy the new collation, and calls retranslate() so the whole UI re-lays out in Japanese.
QML's Accessible attached properties exposed the virtualised list items, tabs, combo box, and sidebar items to AT-SPI on Linux without extra plumbing.
Its GPU scene graph renders on demand through QRhi across OpenGL ES, OpenGL, Vulkan, Metal, or Direct3D.
limits: Licensing is commercial, GPLv3, or dynamically linked LGPLv3, and add-ons such as Qt Graphs and Qt Quick 3D are GPLv3 or commercial only.
QML errors appear only at run time, binding dependencies can drop silently, and lupdate could not parse newer QML pragma syntax without a workaround script.
ListView transitions fire on every model change unless gated by hand, combining reuseItems with transitions left stale delegates, and Qt Charts requires QtWidgets.
Qt offers no portable system query for reduced motion, and Basic style padding and headers made exact pixel pinning fiddly.

prose.fan: You reach for Slint when you want a compiled declarative UI language paired with Rust logic and a stable 1.x API. It covers desktop, mobile, and embedded devices from one markup language, with editor live preview, bundled translations, and AccessKit support built in.
cool: Compiled .slint markup pairs typed properties, repeaters, callbacks, and inline accessibility attributes with a Rust Model for a virtualised ListView.
Translation and plural forms live right in markup through @tr, with PO catalogues bundled into the binary and switched live at run time.
Declarative states with in and out animate declarations move and fade each row's inner body inside its slot, while editor tooling includes a language server and live preview on save.
limits: Licensing offers three options: GPLv3, a royalty-free licence with attribution for proprietary desktop, mobile, and web apps excluding embedded systems, or a commercial licence with embedded pricing from $1.00 per device.
ListView cannot animate row height because rows need equal heights, and globals cannot animate, so the theme switch dropped cross-fading.
Slint lacks a dialog accessibility role, gives no .slint query for reduced motion on Linux, and warnings such as deprecated viewport-* properties fail slint-build.
Its WebAssembly target is not recommended for general-purpose web apps, and accessibility features, IME, and copy-paste are unavailable or missing on the web.

shows.caption: List: a virtualised ListView over a Rust model

prose.fan: You reach for egui when you want an immediate-mode GUI in plain Rust with no reactive layer. State lives in an ordinary struct, the UI reads it each frame, and eframe takes that code to desktop, Android, and the web.
cool: The inbox runs in plain Rust across four files, rebuilding its filtered index only on change and redrawing only on events.
ScrollArea::show_rows virtualises uniform rows out of the box, and animate_bool_with_time drives modal fades and layer scaling inline.
Custom graphics need no separate canvas widget, letting the 12-week bar chart paint bars, gridlines, and labels directly with painter calls.
Enabling AccessKit exposed the controls and only 13 visible list items, with position and set size, over AT-SPI on Linux.
limits: Its README warns that interfaces remain in flux and new releases will have breaking changes, and 0.37 moved APIs such as App::ui and global_style.
The docs read name no translation layer, and egui ships no CJK font, no semibold weight, no icon font, and no system reduced-motion query, requiring manual font loading for Japanese.
Keyboard focus routing is manual, animating row heights required a separate show_viewport path, and a click without prior pointer motion did nothing under X11.
A native-looking interface is an explicit non-goal, and the inbox sorted titles by lowercased strings without locale collation.

shows.caption: Free pick: the bar chart, painted directly

prose.fan: You reach for GPUI when you want the GPU-accelerated Rust UI framework of the Zed editor, with Tailwind-like builder chains and explicit entity state. Paired with gpui-kit, you build views with theme switching, dialogs, and selects in plain Rust, with AccessKit through gpui-pre's Linux backend and hand-set roles.
cool: Chained Rust builder methods put layout, styling, focus tracking, accessibility roles, and keyboard handlers on one element tree.
v_virtual_list accepts per-row sizes, letting the inbox virtualise the list while growing and shrinking an animating row.
Views subscribe to entities and call cx.notify explicitly, and theme switching, the dialog, the select, and the bar chart were all easy to build.
With the AT-SPI bus flag set by hand, AccessKit exposed 3 page tabs and a list with only 13 visible list items, one with the SELECTED state.
limits: GPUI is pre-1.0, tied to Zed, and changes signatures often, while the main gpui crate was stale enough that the inbox relied on a gpui-pre snapshot through gpui-kit.
Documentation is thin enough that the implementer read crate sources to use controls, and there is no built-in i18n, collation, or date, number, and plural formatting.
Its global reduce-motion switch snaps animations instead of keeping fades, forcing custom frame tweens, and a focused caret blinks forever unless an idle timeout is configured.
Accessibility roles must be wired by hand, gpui-kit offers no application-wide RTL switch, and mobile platforms are not claimed.

shows.caption: List: a virtual list with per-row sizes and key handling

prose.fan: You reach for Iced when you want a type-safe, cross-platform Rust GUI with an Elm-inspired message-and-update architecture. State changes pass through one typed handler, side effects return as tasks, and rendering runs on wgpu with a tiny-skia fallback across desktop and the web.
cool: Routing every interaction through a Message enum and an update function that returns a Task keeps state flow obvious.
Subscribing to window::frames only while an animation runs keeps an idle window from redrawing.
A dedicated canvas widget made the 12-week bar chart simple, and cosmic-text rendered Japanese with no font setup.
limits: Iced 0.14 has no AccessKit integration, so nothing appeared in AT-SPI and screen readers cannot use it, while unfocusable buttons left Tab order and dialog focus return unmet.

It lacks a virtualised list, text ellipsis, text selection, transforms, and i18n, forcing hand-written spacer windowing, manual title truncation, overlay fades, and a rising dialog instead of scaling.
Its README calls it experimental software, APIs shifted between 0.13 and 0.14, and the implementer had to read crate source to match the new signatures.

shows.caption: State: the Elm architecture's update

prose.fan: You reach for Flutter when you want a Dart widget tree, stable since 1.0 in December 2018, where the engine draws every pixel across mobile, desktop, and web. Impeller, animation widgets, form validation, ICU localization, debug hot reload, and widget tests support building interfaces in Dart.
cool: Flutter widgets, the separate material_ui package, and intl covered the inbox exercised in widget tests, pairing AnimatedList, AnimatedSwitcher, showGeneralDialog, and live Form validation with CustomPainter for the bar chart.
ARB files, gen-l10n, and intl provide ICU plurals, locale number and date formatting, and live language switching, while Directionality supports RTL.

Two widget tests drove the full session at 1280 by 800 and found two bugs the screenshots had not: a sidebar ListTile inside a ColoredBox that hid the selected colour, and the missing Cupertino delegate for ja.
Isolate.run parses the JSON fixture off the UI isolate.
limits: Dart's core libraries lack a locale-aware collator, so the inbox sorted titles by lowercased code units instead of locale collation.
Moving Material 3 into the separate material_ui package churned APIs and caused ambiguous localization delegates, and a widget test found a missing Japanese Cupertino delegate.
On Linux desktop, apps depend on GTK and ship engine shared libraries alongside a generated C++ runner.
The session ran only in widget tests rather than with live sandbox pointer input, and neither AT-SPI output nor CJK glyph rendering was verified on Linux.

shows.caption: Motion: a tab change that fades and slides

prose.fan: You reach for Declare when you want a declarative UI language where reactive constraints, datasets, springs, and standard controls make replication and virtualisation one line. Its UI tree compiles ahead of time for the browser and ships with a live editor and inspector.
cool: The entire inbox spans inbox.declare and inbox-data.ts with no third-party libraries beyond Declare's own controls.

A derived Dataset handles filtering, searching, and sorting declaratively, and virtualising the 10 000-row Table takes one attribute, with Chromium's accessibility tree counting 23 rows, the visible window only.
The bar chart is plain replicated views bound to a dataset computed only on the Insights tab, with accessibility labels on each bar.
Built-in tooling includes a side-by-side live editor, an overlay inspector, and declare-verify checks.
limits: It is pre-1.0 at version 0.7.1 with a small ecosystem, frequent releases where a breaking change is always a release, no packaging story for its macOS host, and no other native desktop target named in the guide read.
Strict compiler rules, Table internals during row-height animation, and default Dialog positioning added friction, while DataSource required wrapping the fixture JSON under a named root.
Built-in Spring physics only approximate fixed millisecond durations, and the guide read names no message catalogue, plural API, or runtime-language feature.
Canvas rendering is opaque to screen readers, declare-verify's boot check could not run in the sandbox, and accessibility was not verified with a real screen reader.

shows.caption: List: a library Table with a virtualized row class

prose.fan: You reach for Solid when you want TypeScript and JSX without a virtual DOM. Components run once, JSX compiles to direct DOM updates, and fine-grained signals and memos track what they read automatically so only the expressions that read a signal re-run.
cool: The inbox is written in TypeScript, TSX, and CSS, with createMemo keeping sorting separate from per-keystroke filtering without dependency arrays.

Solid renders plain DOM, so accessibility is the browser's own, alongside a native dialog, Web Animations API row transitions, inline SVG bars, Intl.Collator sorting, and a virtualised list where only the visible window is in Chromium's accessibility tree.
Each validation rule is a memo over the field's signal, with error text, the live n/120 counter, and ARIA validity attributes bound to those memos as you type.
limits: Solid 2.0 broke 1.x ecosystem packages, leaving @tanstack/solid-virtual unusable and forcing a custom adapter over @tanstack/virtual-core.

Solid 2.0 API shifts such as split createEffect, microtask-batched writes, onSettled, and string ARIA booleans added friction, while 2.0 support in community devtools and the new Vite plugin's HMR remained unverified.
Neither Solid nor @solid-primitives/i18n provides plural or ICU rules, so plurals were branched by hand, and Solid does not claim native desktop or mobile targets.

shows.caption: List: the virtualised listbox

prose.fan: You reach for Leptos when you want Rust compiled to WebAssembly with fine-grained DOM reactivity and no virtual DOM overhead. Components run once, signals are Copy + 'static, and the same toolkit covers client-side apps, server-side rendering with hydration, HTTP streaming, and server functions.
cool: Each row and form field runs once and binds reactive closures directly to individual DOM attributes, ARIA states, and text nodes without component reruns.
Validation rules in the edit form are plain derived closures over local RwSignal fields, updating error text, counters, and Save state automatically.
Paired with leptos_i18n, translation keys are checked at compile time and switch to Japanese live, while Chromium's aria snapshot has 64 rows and both Chromium's and Firefox's errors are empty.
limits: Leptos is pre-1.0, its generic native rendering plan was shelved with no official desktop or mobile claim found on the pages fetched, core ships no i18n, and windowing was hand-written after leptos-use was tried and removed.
Because <For> removes a row at once, animated removals needed a timed ghost row, and closures still needed explicit clones for the borrow checker.

leptos_i18n required rendering interpolated messages as views under load_locales, passing plural counts as closures, duplicating _one keys for Japanese, and touching Rust files so Cargo noticed locale edits.

Full stripping broke wasm-opt by dropping target_features, data-integrity="none" was set to avoid a Chromium console warning, and the implementer read leptos_i18n 0.6.4's sources, its book, and Leptos's macros to debug.

shows.caption: A row: one memo and reactive attribute closures

prose.fan: You reach for Dioxus when you want a fullstack Rust app framework for web, desktop, and mobile with terse rsx markup, signals, and dx serve hot-reloading markup and styles. The README describes a "full-time core team", and it brings HTML, CSS, and Rust components together.
cool: The rsx macro lets you write Rust for loops and if branches directly inside markup, with terse signals and cheap hot-path updates.
Signals, memos, async use_resource, and component reruns let live form validation live in plain let bindings that recompute when a signal changes.
Built-in dx tooling hot-reloads markup and styles with experimental Rust hot-patching, while the public/ directory copies the fixture data to the dist root around dx's hashed asset names.
Native HTML controls, dialog, inline SVG, and ARIA attributes ran with empty error lists in Chromium and Firefox and produced a Chromium aria snapshot with 59 rows.
limits: Dioxus is pre-1.0, its native WGPU renderer remains experimental, and desktop and mobile targets rely on webviews by default.
It ships no built-in list virtualiser, no list exit-transition hook, and no core i18n, requiring hand-written windowing and a timed ghost row for animated removals.
The community dioxus-i18n crate emitted Fluent Unicode bidi isolate characters around interpolated values with no toggle to disable them, forcing a custom stripping wrapper.
Static string keys are rejected, Dioxus.toml schema changes caused errors, setting root attributes required web-sys, and the implementer read crate sources to debug.

shows.caption: The edit form: validation recomputed on every render

prose.fan: You reach for Sycamore when you want fine-grained Rust reactivity in WebAssembly with no virtual DOM and a builder-like view syntax. Signal handles are Copy, components do not rerun on updates, and a Copy store keeps derived memos updated without cloning boilerplate.
cool: A Copy store of signals and memos passes into handlers with no cloning boilerplate, keeping the filtered list, tags, selection position, chart bins, and form checks in sync.
Each changing DOM attribute and ARIA state binds its own closure, updating only the touched node on every keystroke.

Direct web-sys, js-sys, and create_node_ref interop were easy for the native dialog and Intl formatting, while a catalog memo follows the language signal as context for live Fluent language switching.
limits: Sycamore is pre-1.0 with a single crates.io owner, exploratory native and TUI targets, no maintained virtual-list crate, and no i18n API on the pages fetched.

The implementer read framework source to diagnose three runtime pitfalls: RefCell borrow panics when reading memos inside with, browser timers running outside the reactive scope without run_in, and hidden release panics under panic abort.
The view macro wraps non-literal expressions in FnMut closures that trip the borrow checker, lacks an attr directive, and leaves Keyed rows non-reactive in their item data.
Enabling the suspense feature was required just to use spawn_local_scoped, Trunk needed custom wasm-opt flags, and accessibility was not tested with a real screen reader.

shows.caption: Free pick: validation as you type, in view!

prose.fan: You reach for Yew when you want Rust in the browser with function components, hooks, reducers, and JSX-like markup. First published in 2017, it pairs an immutable reducer store and ContextProvider with virtual DOM diffing and PartialEq prop checks.
cool: A single use_reducer store with Rc-shared records and ContextProvider fits this app, returning the same Rc to skip re-renders when nothing changes.
Keyed rows with PartialEq props keep unchanged virtualised items from re-rendering, and no framework source reading was needed to build the app.
Direct web-sys and js-sys interop covered the native dialog, Intl.Collator sorting, inline SVG, and ARIA attributes, where the Chromium accessibility snapshot counted 76 rows, as did Firefox.
limits: Yew remains pre-1.0 after a gap of about 26 months between 0.21 and 0.22, with experimental SSR, work-in-progress testing support, and native desktop or mobile targets not claimed on the pages fetched.
Ecosystem crates lag behind 0.23, with yew-i18n targeting 0.21 and no maintained virtual-list crate, forcing fluent-bundle and hand-written list windowing.

Nodes are removed immediately with no exit-transition hook, requiring a timed ghost row, while the html macro rejects textarea children, lacks attribute spread, and needs hand-stringified ARIA values.
Trunk's default wasm-opt rejected rustc 1.98 output without manual feature flags, full stripping caused wasm-bindgen warnings, and accessibility was not tested with a real screen reader.

shows.caption: State: one reducer, every change an Action

frameworks.name: Dioxus (desktop)

prose.fan: The Dioxus web inbox built for Dioxus's desktop renderer: the same components and CSS, with the VirtualDom in a native Rust process and the DOM in the system WebView (wry over WebKitGTK). Data is read from disk at start-up and avatars come through an asset handler; DOM access goes through eval instead of web-sys. The window is undecorated, because GTK 3 draws its own title bar on Wayland. Title sort is a lowercase compare, not locale-aware, since the WebView's collator is only reachable asynchronously. A one-round smoke measured 2.9 % idle CPU, from WebKit's processes.

frameworks.strategy: Dioxus desktop renderer: VirtualDom in a native Rust process, DOM in the system WebView (wry/WebKitGTK)

frameworks.name: Dioxus (native, Blitz)

prose.fan: The Dioxus desktop inbox on Dioxus's native renderer: the same VirtualDom and stylesheet, styled and laid out by Blitz and drawn by vello, with no WebView and no JS engine. It renders, then crashes in most bench runs: removing a node does not drop its CSS animations, and the next restyle indexes the removed node, an upstream Blitz bug. The CSS transitions were kept, since dropping motion would hide the bug and break parity. Anything that went through eval (dialog, theme, focus) does nothing.

frameworks.strategy: Rust VirtualDom, Blitz CSS layout, vello GPU drawing
missing: settings dialog, focus, scroll restore, system theme/motion (eval is a no-op); locale collation

frameworks.name: Ljós on the web (wasm kernel)

prose.fan: The ljos-web app with its sources byte for byte, built with the wasm kernel: Ljós's own reactive core (ljos_reactive) runs the bindings, and Solid only renders. Where WebAssembly does not run, the page falls back to Solid's signals. 19 of 20 steps answered, as in the ljos-web entry, with heavier steps (new issue 163 ms against 64).

frameworks.strategy: qmlc AOT to Solid, wasm reactive kernel (LJOS_KERNEL=wasm)

frameworks.name: Ljós compiled in the browser

prose.fan: The ljos-web app's QML is not compiled at build time: the page fetches the 15 .qml files and the TypeScript, compiles them with the wasm compiler in 155 to 164 ms, links the result against the page's runtime and mounts it. That is the path an editor's preview, or a program that changes its own QML, takes. The runtime's module list is kept whole as the docs ship it, which is why the start takes 156 requests. Every session step answered.

frameworks.strategy: QML compiled in the browser by the wasm compiler (ljos-web/compiler), Solid kernel

frameworks.name: Declare (canvas)

prose.fan: The Declare inbox with its source unchanged; only the renderer differs from the DOM entry. Its pictures match the DOM build's pixel for pixel, including the app's own quirks (off-centre identicons, an overhanging Japanese Close button). 19 of 20 session steps answered; after the settings Close click the session saw no frame change, not traced.

missing: close settings click showed no change

frameworks.name: Qt Quick on the web

prose.fan: The native Qt Quick inbox compiled against Qt's WebAssembly kit; one wasm holds QtCore, Gui, Qml, Quick, Controls (Basic), the compiled QML, both translations and the app. The page fetches the fixture, avatars and shared Noto subsets and writes them into Emscripten's in-memory file system, so the C++ data code is the native build's byte for byte. A Japanese fallback is registered because Qt on wasm cannot reach the browser's fonts. In one smoke run every session step answered; not yet in the measured results.

frameworks.strategy: Qt Quick + C++ compiled with emscripten, drawn into one WebGL canvas (single-threaded)
missing: no list rows in the browser a11y tree (harness a11y_rows 0); reduced motion from the checkbox only (no media query); system theme via Qt style hints; 25 MB wasm (9.3 MB gzip); Japanese from the shared Noto subsets

frameworks.name: Slint on the web

prose.fan: The native Slint UI files unchanged, with Rust that fetches the issues and the 24 avatars over HTTP and decodes the PNGs itself, since there is no file system. An imported font is not a glyph fallback in Slint 1.19, so the Noto Sans CJK subset is the default family and draws Latin too, with a Bold face for the heavy weights. The fonts are compiled into the wasm. All 20 session steps answered.

frameworks.strategy: Slint markup + Rust compiled to wasm, drawn into one WebGL2 canvas
missing: no accessibility reaches the browser; theme cross-fade dropped; IME unchecked; winit control-flow exception logged as console error

frameworks.name: egui on the web

prose.fan: The native egui app's source, fetched over HTTP instead of read from disk: issues, avatars and a Japanese font subset arrive with ehttp. Everything is drawn into one WebGL2 canvas through glow, chosen over wgpu for a smaller wasm that needs no WebGPU. egui ships no CJK glyphs and a canvas cannot reach the browser's fonts, so a shared Noto Sans JP subset is loaded as a fallback. All 20 session steps answered in Chromium's software path.

frameworks.strategy: Rust immediate-mode UI compiled to wasm, drawn into one WebGL2 canvas
missing: no a11y tree on web (TTS only); no reduced-motion query; lowercase title collation

frameworks.name: Iced on the web

prose.fan: The native Iced app with std time swapped for web time and its data, avatars and fonts fetched at boot. Nothing is drawn until fonts and issues have arrived, because a pick list keeps the text it shaped first. Fonts are shared Noto subsets: Iced's web default, Fira Sans, has no semibold and none of the app's symbols. wgpu runs on its WebGL2 backend. All 20 session steps answered.

frameworks.strategy: Rust Elm-style UI compiled to wasm, drawn into one WebGL2 canvas
missing: no accessibility at all; no Tab focus order or focus return; dialog fade+rise instead of scale; lowercase title collation

frameworks.name: Flutter on the web (CanvasKit)

prose.fan: The native Flutter app with dart:io and isolates replaced: the fixture is fetched and decoded on the page's thread, and avatars are network images. CanvasKit is served locally rather than from Google's CDN, the Noto fonts are bundled because a canvas sees no system fonts, and the engine's font fallback points at a local path so a missing glyph never reaches a CDN. 19 of 20 session steps answered.

frameworks.strategy: Dart compiled to JS, Skia (CanvasKit wasm) draws into one WebGL canvas
missing: semantics off until the user enables them (0 a11y rows); close-issue click misses (content centred, native code); 閉じる wraps; 1.3–1.7 s frame while search filters

frameworks.name: Flutter on the web (skwasm)

prose.fan: The same source as the CanvasKit build, compiled with --wasm. Measured on a server sending COOP and COEP, where the page is cross-origin isolated and Chromium loads skwasm and main.dart.wasm. The build keeps main.dart.js and CanvasKit as the fallback for browsers without WasmGC. 19 of 20 session steps answered; the first key typed into search shows nothing for 1.5 to 2.2 s, where CanvasKit takes 56 ms.

frameworks.strategy: Dart compiled to WasmGC, Skia (skwasm, multi-threaded under COOP/COEP) draws into one canvas
missing: as canvaskit; first search key press answers in 1.5–2.2 s

prose.fan: Qt Quick's inbox with its logic in Rust: QML UI + Rust logic via CXX-Qt.

frameworks.name: CXX-Qt
frameworks.strategy: QML UI + Rust logic via CXX-Qt
missing: C++ glue (71 lines) for translator, style, image provider, loadFromModule

prose.fan: Qt Quick's inbox with its logic in Rust: QML UI + Rust logic via Qt Bridge.

frameworks.name: Qt Bridge
frameworks.strategy: QML UI + Rust logic via Qt Bridge

features.label: Virtualised list
features.about: 10 000 issues, and rows made only for the ones in view.

ljos.code:
ListView {
    id: view
    objectName: "issues"
    x: 0
    y: 32
    width: pane.width
    height: pane.height - 32
    clip: true
    focus: true
    model: pane.inbox.rows
    key: "id"
